title: House Spirits Are the New House Wines
summary:
Instead of relying on what’s available from large distributors, a growing contingent of beverage pros are developing custom house spirits that you can’t find anywhere else.

The post House Spirits Are the New House Wines appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Bartenders are moving past standard distributor bottles to create proprietary, house-made spirits for truly unique cocktail programs.
  • Establishments collaborate with distilleries to capture distinct flavors that speak to the cuisine.

A bartender’s toolkit is pretty much the same no matter where you work. It’s a mix of classic spirits and dasher bottles of bitters, plus a few liqueurs, amari, and fresh ingredients to play around with.

That’s been the case for generations. But now as bartenders get even more creative and push the limits of what can go into a cocktail, many are feeling constrained with existing products that have long been stocked behind every bar in America. So instead of relying on what’s available from large distributors, a growing contingent of beverage pros are opting to develop custom house spirits that you can’t find anywhere else. 

From distinct bottles of Lost Voyager Rum that are only available at Strong Water in Anaheim and Mal Bien mezcal made specially for Mírate and Daisy Margarita Bar in Los Angeles to rare distillates that power cocktails at New York City bars like Oddball, schmuck., and The Dead Rabbit, these one-of-a-kind spirits allow bars to deliver drinks that are truly unique.

Boundary-Pushing Bottles

At Quince, a three-Michelin-starred restaurant in San Francisco, the kitchen morphs produce from its nearby organic farm into ingredient-driven menus that change by the season. When Bar Agricole, a single-origin spirit distillery and former bar, began a limited-time residency at the restaurant in 2024, the team was finally able to get involved in the farm-to-table approach too.

As the two teams explored how to incorporate the farm’s produce behind the bar, they landed on an idea for a bottle that could permanently live on the back bar. “A kernel of an idea started to germinate into a radical one,” says Lead Bartender Craig Lane. “What if we could build a ‘single origin’ gin made exclusively with botanicals from the farm?”

Lane explains that the limited slate of gin available in the U.S. was perplexing to the team because gin uses more plants than any other spirit, yet so few bottles actually harness a sense of place. “So much attention is always given to the proprietary botanicals, which can be sourced from anywhere in the world, and so little attention is given to the industrial-strength grain alcohol without any agricultural provenance,” Lane says.

Together the restaurant and bar launched Bolinas Gin, a tisane-style liquor made with fresh botanicals from Quince’s Fresh Run Farm instead of dried ingredients. The spirit also uses locally grown, biodynamic grape distillate as the base spirit, further distinguishing the flavor because it lends subtle fruity notes and rounder mouthfeel than other commercially available bottles.

That same desire—to unlock flavor profiles that wouldn’t otherwise exist—also led Brooklyn restaurant Golden Ratio to partner with NYC-based sustainable distillery Acid Spirits to make about ten different hyper-local distillates, many of which are produced using waste from the Clinton Hill bar and its sister restaurants.

Each product made by Acid Spirits is vacuum-distilled, allowing the team to produce spirits that show off the nuances of a fresh ingredient. The brand offers a collection of bottles made with everything from coffee grounds and horseradish, but owner Joe McDowell also works with several high-caliber bars and restaurants in NYC (like Smithereens, Gramercy Tavern, and Corima) on custom creations.

“It allows us to have a different DNA for all of our drinks that’s proprietary to us,” Piper Kristensen, Redwood Hospitality partner and beverage director, says. “It makes the creative process of making cocktails a little bit more fun because we’re not limited to pre-existing archetypes and flavor profiles.”

Problem Solved

While most bartenders love to use peak-season fruit and obscure herbs, time, budget, and seasonal availability can make it difficult to pull off. Custom spirits, however, provide a clever solution.

Cove, a seasonal fine-dining restaurant in NYC, currently uses two unique products created in partnership with Acid Spirits: a marigold distillate that’s combined with vermouth and sparkling tea for the Farm Tea Vodka Soda and a spirit made with lemongrass, lemon verbena, and lemon basil used in the restaurant’s riff on a Cosmopolitan.

“Our bar program in a lot of ways is an extension of the kitchen so we want a variety of ways to work with the same herbs and produce that the kitchen team uses,” says Otis Baldwin, Cove’s service director and lead bartender. “That being said, we really try to make drinks that are recognizable for guests and working with Acid allows us to make a drink like a Cosmo our own.”

Iain Griffiths, the owner of Bar Snack in NYC’s East Village, says working with Matchbook Distilling to develop a pine-flavored distillate allowed them to preserve a season in a bottle. “One of distillation’s greatest advantages is that we can utilize it to harness and preserve raw ingredients at a specific moment in time,” Griffiths says.

Without the work of Matchbook’s Leslie Merinoff, Griffiths says the holiday drink they were developing would have been shelved because none of the alpine amari available hit the right flavor note. 

While custom bottles like the Bar Snack x Matchbook Distilling pine tree distillate can help bartenders shave down prep time and round out a recipe, they’re also just plain fun to have on the backbar, Griffiths says.

“Custom spirits have also wound up being like a bartender’s handshake when traveling because each bottle is so special,” Griffiths says. “They have become a beautiful little creative piece to share with somebody.”

title: Celebrate Labor Day with These 6 Hot Dog and Wine Pairings
summary:
Sommeliers recommend the best wine pairings for America's most iconic regional hot dogs, from Chicago style to Michigan Coneys.

The post Celebrate Labor Day with These 6 Hot Dog and Wine Pairings appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Ask six sommeliers what wine they’d pair with a hot dog, and you’ll get six different answers. 

A Chicago-style dog topped with tomatoes, pickles, and peppers has little in common with a chili-smothered Michigan Coney or a bacon-wrapped Sonoran dog. Given that the flavors, textures, and aromas of these regional hot dogs are wildly different, the wines that complement them are, too.

Ask those same sommeliers how they might approach pairing wine with a hot dog, and some consensus starts to emerge. “When I’m pairing wine with a hot dog, I actually let the toppings be my guiding factor,” says Phoenix-based sommelier Samantha Capaldi. Rather than focusing on the protein, she considers acidity, smoke, sweetness, spice, richness, and texture. “From there, I fine-tune the pairing to find a wine that complements the whole bite, not just the sausage.”

Clara Klein, lead sommelier for Frasca Hospitality Group in Colorado, agrees. “The sausage brings salty, savory richness, but the toppings are usually the real main character,” she says. “Figure out which basic flavors and textures are doing the heavy lifting, and the wine choice becomes surprisingly easy.” 

In other words, the wines may vary, but the guiding principles remain the same. As you fire up the grill, consider pairing any of these iconic regional hot dogs with the perfect wine.

New York Hot Dog: Off-Dry Riesling

Follow the acidity. Tangy toppings call for bright, refreshing wines that won’t be bullied by mustard and sauerkraut.

The New York hot dog may be one of the simplest regional styles, but its classic toppings—spicy brown mustard and either sauerkraut or tomato-based onion sauce—put acidity front and center. Rather than reaching for a heavy red, several sommeliers suggested wines with enough brightness to stand up to those punchy condiments without overwhelming the frank itself.

“The topping that I’m focused on here is the spicy brown mustard, which will make a dry wine taste bitter,” says Daniela DaSuta, wine educator and founder of SommSpace. She recommends an off-dry German Riesling for its generous acidity balanced by a touch of sweetness. “[It] will calm the spice and will seem refreshing.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Sybille Kuntz 2018 Spätlese Trocken (Mosel)

This is flavorful and well balanced, with beautiful acidity backing the ripe palate of orange, yellow apple and cardamom notes, with a firm minerality emerging on the finish. Good length. 92 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$50 Solano Cellars

More Great Options: Other sommeliers took a similar approach, even if they landed on different bottles. Klein recommends Sangiovese for its bright acidity and savory edge, while Mark Guillaideu, Master Sommelier at Eleven Madison Park, reaches for Nerello Mascalese. “[It’s] bright, punchy, with plenty of acidity and tannin from its parent Sangiovese but a deeper and more meat-forward savor,” he says. Allegra Angelo, owner of Vinya Wine Shop and Bar, instead opts for Etna Bianco, whose mineral drive and richness she says are bold enough to stand up to the hot dog’s bold toppings.

Shop Now

Chicago Dog: Sancerre

Herbaceous, crisp wines shine alongside vegetables, pickles, and peppers.

The Chicago dog is one of America’s most topping-driven hot dogs. With tomatoes, pickles, relish, sport peppers, celery salt, and onions piled onto an all-beef frank, it’s basically a condiment sandwich. With so many crunchy, savory things going on, fresh, herbaceous wines are a natural fit.

“This style of hot dog has ‘salad bar’ stamped on its bun, making it a home run for a medium-plus-bodied Sauvignon Blanc, which naturally gravitates into those herbal tones,” says Angelo. That herbaceous thread runs through nearly every recommendation. Capaldi reaches for Sancerre.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Domaine Girault 2023 Chêne Marchand Sauvignon Blanc (Sancerre)

This is an attractive Sancerre. Aromas of bread dough, muddled bosc pear, and golden apple charm the nose along with orange zest and baby’s breath. The palate is well-integrated with orchard fruit shining through supported by crushed stones and chalk-dusted acidity that refreshes. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Reggie Solomon

$40 Spiro Wines

Another Great Option: Klein opts for Grüner Veltliner, which “has peppery notes and plenty of acidity,” she says. “[It] was born for crunchy vegetables, pickles and peppers.”

In the shop

Riedel Veloce Sauvignon Blanc Wine Glasses (Set of 2)

In Stock | $99

Shop Now

Michigan Coney: Alsace Pinot Gris

Choose wines with enough fruit and freshness to balance the rich, savory topping.

The Michigan Coney layers a snappy frank with savory meat sauce, mustard, and onions, a rich combination that seems like a natural set-up for red wine. Most sommeliers agreed, gravitating toward fruit-forward reds—perhaps served with a chill—with enough freshness to keep the whole thing from feeling too heavy. 

In the shop

Wine Enthusiast Somm Pinot Noir Handblown Wine Glass

In Stock | $45

Shop Now

Angelo, however, takes a boldly different approach. “You could almost veer into red with this kind of hot dog,” she says. “Instead, reach for a red wine lover’s white,” recommending a dry Pinot Gris from Alsace. “What it lacks in acid, it more than makes up for in texture, wintry spices, baked orchard fruit, and marmalade earthiness—all qualities that exist for sausage-style meats.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Trimbach 2018 Réserve Pinot Gris (Alsace)

Only a hint of freshly cut, ripe pear peel appears briefly on the nose of this wine. The palate presents a precise picture of concentrated ripe, green pear that comes with purity, precision and restraint. All the fruit is there, but rather than rounding out, it soars with freshness, which is a real achievement in 2018. The finish is dry and vivid. 92 Points — Anne Krebiehl MW

$38 67 Wine & Spirits

More Great Options: If red wines are more your speed for this kind of hot dog, you’ll find plenty of company. Primitivo, Cru Beaujolais, Grenache, and Nero d’Avola all surfaced as recommendations. “I’d love to try this with a traditional style Reserva Rioja, especially if the dog is ‘Detroit style,’ with a cumin-based sauce with beef and beef hearts,” says Gaither. “The Rioja would have lovely stewed red and black fruit flavors, with notes of toasted coconut and dill plus some earthiness that would offset the richness of the toppings, and freshen up each bite of the dog.”

Sonoran Dog: Rosé Champagne

With so many toppings, choose wines that refresh rather than overpower.

Wrapped in bacon and topped with pinto beans, avocado, tomatoes, onions, mayonnaise, mustard, and salsa, the Sonoran hot dog is almost embarrassingly over the top. “This is the nacho hot dog,” says Angelo. “Rather than asking the wine to compete for the flavor stage, I’d let it take a step back.” While she recommends an Alpine white like a Vin de Savoie, the bigger takeaway is this: don’t ask your wine to out-muscle this hot dog.  

For Capaldi, this pairing is personal. “I have to pair this one with a dry rosé because it’s pure nostalgia for me,” she says. “I went to college in Tucson, Arizona, and I have so many memories of grabbing a Sonoran dog and enjoying it with a cheap bottle of rosé. To this day, it’s still one of my favorite pairings.” 

In the shop

Wine Enthusiast Vienna Break-Resistant Champagne Glasses

In Stock | $50

Shop Now

Klein also gravitates toward rosé, but with bubbles. “Bacon, beans, avocado, and mayo? There’s a lot going on here,” she says. “Rosé Champagne is the perfect foil: its vibrant bubbles cut through the layers of richness, while its bright red fruit complements the fresh salsa.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Billecart-Salmon NV Le Rosé Extra Brut Sparkling Blend (Champagne)

The nose is delicate and ripe, showing sweet raspberry, lemon curd patisserie, and orange blossom. The palate mirrors that delicacy with wild strawberry, raspberry, grapefruit, citrus zest, tangerine oil, wildflowers, and soft clay-chalky minerality lingering on the finish. Enjoy now with rich sashimi and keep a few in cellar and wait for more nuance to emerge. 93 Points — Anna-Christina Cabrales

$100 Total Wine

Another Great Option: Gaither’s recommendation may be the boldest—and most passionate—of the bunch. “Going out on a limb here, but if you’ve never had aged German Spätlese Riesling—I’m talking, like, 15 years old or more—with one of these Sonoran dogs, you’re not living your fullest life! Trust me, this is world changing!”

Cincinnati Coney: Grenache

Reach for juicy, spice-friendly reds with enough freshness to handle the cheddar.

Forget all your assumptions about a chili dog. The Cincinnati Coney is topped with the city’s signature cinnamon- and clove-laced chili, along with mustard, onions, and a generous mound of finely shredded cheddar. The cozy flavor combination calls for something a little different in the glass. 

“My husband is from Ohio, so when someone says ‘a generous mound’ of cheese, I’ve learned that means well beyond the doctor’s recommended daily allowance,” says Angelo. She suggests a Grenache from Paso Robles. “It’s nearly impossible not to fall in love with Grenache’s sweet and smoky fruit, melt-away tannins, and velvety texture. It’s mind-bogglingly delicious with meat and somehow works with cheese. Just give the bottle twenty minutes in the refrigerator to feel, at least, a little bougie.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Terranean Wines 2023 Grenache (Paso Robles)

This newer brand by husband-and-wife vintners Alex and Ryan Kemp is off to a tremendous start. This appellation cuvée is clean and precise on the nose with pure cherry, rose candy and baking spice aromas. The palate is juicy, generous and complex, showing cherry, mocha, nut-spiced coffee and rooibos tea flavors that are enveloped in a leathery grip. Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — Matt Kettmann

$65 Terranean Wines

More Great Options: Others echoed the importance of matching the chili’s spice profile. Capaldi reaches for a GSM blend, while Klein loves chilled Lambrusco, whose bubbles and juicy dark fruit refresh the palate between bites while complementing the Mediterranean-leaning flavors of the chili.

Zalto Denk’Art Burgundy Glass

In Stock | $85

Shop Now

D.C. Half-Smoke: Syrah

Peppery reds—or savory aged whites—can stand up to the sausage.

The D.C. Half-Smoke is unapologetically bold, with a smoky sausage, mustard, onions, and often a generous ladle of chili. Unsurprisingly, many sommeliers suggested Syrah and its relatives, whose peppery spice and savory character naturally mirror the sausage itself.

“I love Syrah so much that I named my son Rhone,” says DaSuta, recommending either Rhône Syrah or Australian Shiraz. “The smoky, peppery sausage is a natural match for the gamey qualities of Syrah, which will also start to smell like smoked meat as it ages.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Yann Chave 2023 Syrah (Crozes-Hermitage)

The nose is strikingly pure with cassis, blackberry and a graceful thread of garrigue, echoing the thoughtful effort put into this wine. The palate’s bright acidity energizes its dark, supple fruit and extends into a refined stony, fine-herb finish. Approachable now, yet destined to gain even more nuance with time. Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — A.C.C.

$30 Mr. D Wine Merchants

More Great Options: Not everyone reached for red, though. Angelo makes the case for an aged Timorasso, a textured white from Italy’s Piedmont region, arguing that the mustard calls for freshness while bottle age brings enough savory complexity to stand up to the sausage. “At first glance, I’m thinking about a red, yet mustard begs for refreshment,” she says. “So, my compromise is a white wine with age.”

Latitude Wine Cellars: Versatile Storage for Every Collection

By JULIE SPACE

Every wine collection is unique, yet many cellar shelves force you into a rigid, one-size-fits-all approach that simply doesn’t work with the diverse storage needs of your growing inventory.

As you acquire more than just Bordeaux-style bottles, standard shelves become less than ideal, causing tight, awkward stacking and scraped labels. An expanding portfolio—and palate—calls for a more flexible solution. 

Latitude was designed for that reality, with universal shelving that accommodates a multitude of bottle types, from broad-shouldered Pinot Noirs to long, tapered Rieslings. 

“One of the biggest frustrations for wine collectors is not having the flexibility to store the bottles they love,” says Stuart Diamond, Wine Enthusiast’s Senior Category Director, Wine Storage. “Latitude is an excellent upgrade for those who have outgrown their first wine fridge, offering adaptable storage and more sophisticated features.”

title: Bordeaux Estates Helped Fight the Fires—But a New Battle Begins
summary:
The wildfires that blazed through Southwest France have mostly spared Bordeaux’s vines, but growers remain on edge about a hotter, drier future.

The post Bordeaux Estates Helped Fight the Fires—But a New Battle Begins appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Massive wildfires burned 103,000 acres near Bordeaux, forcing evacuations and threatening nearby towns and key infrastructure.
  • Local winemakers dispatched equipment and staff to assist exhausted firefighters, successfully protecting the region’s major vineyards from fire.
  • Bordeaux growers expect an early 2026 harvest with minimal smoke taint, though long-term climate threats and declining tourism worry producers.

One of the most arresting images to come out of the wildfires that have threatened the Bordeaux vineyards is of horses.

The viral video shows a herd, set free to escape the fire, racing down a street in the village of Biscarosse, away from the cloud of smoke and the raging orange flames. While all the horses are safe, the scene epitomizes the drama that has been unfolding in southwest France.

Fires have burned up 103,000 acres of pine forest and small villages   close to the Atlantic coast of France, sending residents and tourists fleeing and threatening the city’s outer suburbs and major aerospace and military facilities.

While there was no immediate threat to vineyards north and south of the city, in the Médoc and Graves regions, there is real concern from the smoke spread by the winds from the fires. Owners have so far reported no fire losses. Bordeaux vineyards sprawl across 233,000 acres, covering five times more ground than Napa Valley.

An optimistic Philippe Castéja, president of the Conseil des Grands Crus, points out that “no vineyard has been touched and experts have said there is no noticeable effect on the vines.” Guillaume Gonfrier at Vignobles Gonfrier in the southern Entre-deux-Mers, an hour east of Bordeaux center, told us, “I remain confident in the 2026 vintage.” 

While the fires are certainly not out (that process will take months), they are contained. And while the region’s growers may still be on edge, they can breathe a sigh of relief. 

But as Europe gets hotter and drier, and fires become more frequent, Bordeaux estates can’t help but worry about what comes next.

A Wine Community Joins the Firefight

As the blaze spread at an alarming pace, most intensely between July 25 and 29, the region’s elite vineyards didn’t just sit back—they actively joined the firefight. 

Winemakers dispatched tractors to haul water, offered private water cisterns to local crews, sent farm staff to the front lines, and set up coordinated estate networks to respond to new outbreaks. Vine growers rushed to help the stressed and exhausted firefighters with offers of equipment and distributing water.

South of Bordeaux city, at Château Haut-Bailly in Pessac-Léognan, director Véronique Sanders said on Wednesday it was “heartening to see how all the growers are coming to help fight the fire.” Although, she emphasized, the fires have shaken the community. “We had a little smoke on Saturday and now we don’t know if the fires will flair up again,” she said. The vineyards were not affected by fire.

At nearby Château Smith Haut Lafitte, director general Fabien Teitgen says the property has a number of water cisterns they have “put at the disposal of the local firefighters.” They also have emergency plans to remove the animals in their farm but the fire did not come close.

Further north, at Château Margaux, deputy managing director Aurélien Vallance, says the estate has sent staff to assist the firefighters. At Château Giscours in Margaux, they sent tractors and other equipment to ferry water to the firefighters. Says Vallance: “We are working closely with other estates to coordinate any response if the fires should come closer.”

The State of the Harvest

Bordeaux wine country may have averted immediate and catastrophic disaster, but what of the 2026 harvest?

Because of the increasingly hot, dry weather, it will be an exceptionally early one. “We could start harvesting the whites for Pavillon Blanc in about 10 days [on August 10], and for the reds by the end of August,” says Vallance. The risk then is any smoke could affect the red grapes in particular.

Thankfully, wine growers of Bordeaux play down the risk of smoke taint for the harvest. “It’s nothing like what happened in California with the 2020 vintage,” says Vallence.

More worrying is what happens in the future. Because of climate change, Europe is already showing that it is heating fast, faster than other continents. The summer of 2026, already hot and dry, is a sign of the future. The effect will be earlier harvests with the risks of over-ripe grapes that lack the balance that makes Bordeaux so enticing. 

Moreover, at a time when the Bordeaux wine sector was already struggling with plunging consumption, a hit to tourism could be grave. “Tourism was really the only dynamic part of the business that was still growing, both for us and, more generally, for Bordeaux wines,” winemaker Edouard le Grix de la Salle told PBS. “And now this comes along as a brake.”

title: A Beloved Italian Liqueur Is Finally Available in the U.S.—and It’s a Spritz Lover’s Dream
summary:
Sarti Rosa has landed in the U.S., and it's about to become your new favorite spritz.

The post A Beloved Italian Liqueur Is Finally Available in the U.S.—and It’s a Spritz Lover’s Dream appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
A cult-favorite Italian liqueur has finally become available in the United States.

As of July 2026, the frenzy over Sarti Rosa reached a fever pitch as it officially hit American shelves. Made by the Campari Group, the Italian liqueur has notes of blood orange, passionfruit, and mango and is touted as a lighter, sweeter version of Aperol. 

The buzz over the once-hard-to-find Sarti began in 2025 after content creator Eli Rallo posted a TikTok lamenting its scarcity in domestic markets. While the United Kingdom and other European countries enjoyed their “Sarti Summer,” the U.S. fell behind. Now, just over a year after her TikTok, Rallo no longer has to order it from overseas: Sarti has landed in America. 

As soon as I heard the news, I knew I had to get my hands on a bottle.

At the doors of Union Square Wines & Spirits, I was stopped in my tracks by a Sarti spritz shrine, in slideshow form.Pictures of Sarti against the Manhattan skyline faded into seaside scenes overlaid with the hashtag “#mysartisummer.” Inside, I was met by another extravagant display, this time made out of bottles. They were not messing around. 

Union Square employees told me that the liqueur had sold out through its distributor, Southern Glazer’s, almost immediately after becoming available to order. Likewise, it had taken off in the store, and employees attribute a large majority of its success to TikTok. 

As I headed home, bounty secured, I was struck by the bottle’s fluorescent, watermelon pink hue. I wanted to paint my nails this color.

Finally, it came time to prepare my Sarti spritz, and hopefully join its legion of fanatics. Cracking into the bottle, the smell was strong and sweet with tropical passionfruit, mango, and guava leading the charge. There’s a vague bubblegum note. It’s somewhat reminiscent of a fruity vape that was probably made with high school tastes in mind. 

Like an Aperol spritz, the Sarti spritz is a classic 3:2:1 ratio of Prosecco to Sarti to sparkling water. As I often do when making an Aperol spritz, I didn’t measure as I poured the Prosecco and Sarti, nor did I use sparkling water. I’m sorry—it was Saturday, and I was relaxing with friends in the sun. This wasn’t a time for measuring.

To my surprise, my senses weren’t flooded by a rush of sugar on my first sip. The blood orange profile shined with a light sweetness and pleasant bitterness, but the tropical fruits are the real stars: Mango, passionfruit, lychee, dragonfruit, and guava came together in harmony. I wished I had a sprig of mint to slap on as a garnish. 

After two spritzes, I was pleasantly, lightly buzzed. At just 14% abv, Sarti makes a spritz that’s light enough to sip on all day without paying too high a price. While it’s definitely fruity, it keeps the sweetness in check and brings just enough bitterness to appeal to a wide range of palates. 

I’m not saying Aperol spritzes are going away anytime soon, but it wouldn’t hurt to give Sarti a try—just make sure to snag a bottle before the TikTok crowd gets to it all. And who knows? You might just end up with a new favorite cocktail.

How to Make a Sarti Spritz

From Sarti Rosa

  • Ice Cubes
  • 3 ounces Prosecco
  • 2 ounces Sarti Rosa
  • 1 ounce Soda Water
  • Slice of Lime
Step 1
Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Step 2
Add 2 parts of Sarti Rosa.
Step 3
Add 3 parts of Prosecco.
Step 4
Garnish with a lime slice.
Step 5
Top with a splash of soda.

title: Why the Difference Between Inland and Coastal Wine Regions Matters
summary:
The average consumer may not consider coastal vs. inland when choosing a bottle of wine, but the difference matters.

The post Why the Difference Between Inland and Coastal Wine Regions Matters appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Despite all the advancements made in winemaking, wine is still very much beholden to the whims of nature. Weather patterns, orientation to the sun, soil hydration, altitude, and countless other natural phenomena influence vines. One major factor is proximity to water:  Vineyards planted near the water are cultivated differently than those situated inland.   

Take Southern California. It’s “a massive region, but the weather is pretty consistent from Los Angeles down to San Diego,” explains Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Matt Kettmann, who reviews wines from the area. Rather, the biggest climate variations happen the further you travel inland. “The main differences are the cooler temperatures, fog, and wind influence on the coastline versus the warmer, 100-plus-degree days that can happen inland.” 

The average consumer may not consider coastal vs. inland when choosing a bottle of wine, but these influences  play an important role in what’s in your glass.  

What Sets Coastal Regions Apart

A coastal region or coastal vineyard is just that: vines that grow near a large body of water. However, coastal vineyards are not necessarily planted on a cliff at water’s edge. They can be near a coast or influenced by the coast, as in the case of South Africa’s Coastal Region, which is within 100 miles of the Southern Ocean.

“Vineyards closer to the ocean are more susceptible to the dynamic weather that comes [off the water] because they are less protected than lower lying vineyards inland,” says Chantal Forthun, winemaker for Flowers Vineyards & Winery on the Sonoma Coast. “A strong gust can bring in cold air and fog and bring the temperature down drastically in only a matter of minutes, so the daily climatic conditions can change on a dime.”  

Many coastal wine regions have a maritime climate, characterized by cool to moderate temperatures. Some vineyards in these regions are planted at high elevations, often above the fog line, which is a viticultural boon. These areas have relatively stable temperatures that affect the grapes’ ripening ability since there’s little diurnal shift, or temperature fluctuation between day and night. 

Crucially, the ocean creates the winds that cool down coastal vineyard sites. Wind is so important in viticulture that many winds have their own names: in South Africa, there’s the Cape Doctor, a southeasterly wind that funnels down the mountains and creates a fog layer that blankets vineyards; in Chile, the Humboldt Current comes up from Antarctica to cool the hot, arid climate. These winds tend to be most prevalent along coastal sites.

What to Expect from Inland Regions 

Because inland vineyards are further away from bodies of water, they don’t benefit from cooling ocean influences. As a result, they tend to be warmer and trap heat.  

If inland valleys and regions are in warm or hot climates, winemakers can rely more heavily on diurnal shift—those extreme day-night temperature swings—to ripen grapes. Cool nights help prevent grapes from losing their natural acidity, resulting in more balanced wines.

Being far from ocean moisture can also result in drier vineyard conditions. Drier vines mean a lower risk of moisture-related ailments, like mildew, but it also increases winemakers’ reliance on rivers and artificial irrigation. 

Many coastal wine regions have a maritime climate, which, according to the Wine & Spirit Education Trust (WSET), “are characterized by cool to moderate temperatures and a low annual difference between the hottest and coldest months.”   

Some coastal vineyards are planted at high elevations, often above the fog line, which is a viticultural boon. These areas have relatively stable temperatures that affect the grapes’ ripening ability since there’s little diurnal swing, or temperature fluctuation between day and night. Vines above the fog line can enjoy sun exposure all day, which is beneficial for ripening.   

Those waves and cool ocean temperatures often dictate the winds that cool down the vineyard sites. Wind is so important in viticulture that many of them have their own names: in South Africa there’s the Cape Doctor, a southeasterly wind that funnels down the mountains and creates a fog layer that blankets vineyards; in Chile, the Humboldt Current comes up from Antarctica to cool the hot, arid climate. These winds tend to be most prevalent along coastal sites and protect the vines in a variety of ways.

title: Polvaro Estate: Discover the Quiet Luxury of Lison Classico
summary:
Less than an hour from the bustle of Venice, a mystical estate blanketed in vine-covered hillsides awaits those with an appetite for the lesser-known. Located in the heart of the Lison Classico DOCG, Polvaro Estate invites wine lovers to experience the magic of northern Italy through its distinctly unique wines, which speak to the hidden

The post Polvaro Estate: Discover the Quiet Luxury of Lison Classico appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Polvaro Estate: Discover the Quiet Luxury of Lison Classico

Less than an hour from the bustle of Venice, a mystical estate blanketed in vine-covered hillsides awaits those with an appetite for the lesser-known. Located in the heart of the Lison Classico DOCG, Polvaro Estate invites wine lovers to experience the magic of northern Italy through its distinctly unique wines, which speak to the hidden gem area of the Veneto from which they come. With roots dating back to 1681, Polvaro Estate comes steeped in regional heritage, beloved for its historic architecture, understated charm, and refreshing, site-reflective wines with centuries-old legacy at their core.

Contrary to Italy’s larger appellations, the Lison Classico DOCG, which is located between Veneto and Friuli, is a hidden jewel appellation defined by elegance, subtlety, and a distinct sense of place. Cradled between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea, this small appellation’s vines are rooted in alluvial plains, which benefit from cool mountain breezes and tempering coastal winds. A mosaic of grape varieties—including Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Friulano, the signature grape of Lison Classico DOCG, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Merlot—thrives in the area’s distinctive cantaro soils.

These special caranto soils—which are a highly compact, ancient calcareous clay— act as a master architect in creating structured yet accessible wines that promise to win the hearts of a myriad of unique preferences. Most importantly, caranto soils naturally restrict yields, leading to immensely concentrated grape clusters; when coupled with mineral-rich earth, the result is white wines with rich, enveloping textures and vibrant mineral tension, along with full-bodied reds defined by muscular structure and complex fruit forwardness.  

Polvaro Estate has been at the helm of the surrounding area’s wine production since 1681, centuries before the area received its official appellation designations. In recent years, the Candoni De Zan family acquired the property, bringing a contemporary breath of fresh air to the historic site. While Armando De Zan and Elviana Candoni De Zan remain actively involved, the estate is increasingly shaped by the presence of their daughters, Barbara and Caterina, who represent a new generation of hands-on female leadership within the wine industry.

Under Barbara and Caterina’s careful oversight, Polvaro Estate has transformed into a haven for quiet luxury and sustainability in the heart of the Veneto region. The sisters’ unique approach is greatly influenced by eight years of upbringing in Atlanta, Georgia—an experience that not only shaped the duo’s hospitality perspective, but also created a natural bridge between Italian heritage and American culture. Both seasoned sommeliers and hospitality visionaries, Barbara and Caterina welcome guests with open arms, believing that sharing convivial moments around a great bottle of wine is one of the profoundest means of human connection—especially when done with warmth, reverence for tradition, and a hands-on family approach.

In addition to their hospitality-forward mentality, sustainability also remains at the heart of Polvaro Estate. The property is SQNPI certified (Sistema di Qualità Nazionale di Produzione Integrata), reflecting an integrated and long-term commitment to responsible viticulture and land stewardship. The certification’s core principles include prioritizing biodiversity, maintaining environmental balance, and leaving the land better for future generations.

Beyond the vines, sustainability and signature Italian charm are equally reflected in the glass. At the heart of Polvaro Estate is Polvaro Nero, the estate’s flagship wine and a contemporary expression of the distinctive landscape between the Adriatic Sea and the pre-Alps. Crafted from the estate’s finest vineyard parcels, including 30-year-old vines with naturally low yields, the wine unites Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Malbec, each vinified separately to preserve the varieties’ individual character before being carefully blended.  Aged for twelve months in French oak and further matured before release, the result is a wine of depth, elegance, and balance—one that reflects both the richness of the land and the thoughtful stewardship of the Candoni De Zan family.

The same philosophy guides the estate’s single-vineyard Polvaro Pinot Grigio DOC Venezia, a refined expression that elevates one of Italy’s most iconic varietals beyond expectations. Sourced from a single vineyard and crafted with meticulous attention to detail, it offers vibrant freshness, layered texture, and remarkable elegance, showcasing the quality potential of DOC Venezia. Together, these wines reflect Polvaro Estate’s commitment to expressing both the character of the land and the family’s contemporary vision.

Upon first sip, wine lovers are immediately greeted by the beauty of northern Italy, as well as immersed in a way of life characterized by quiet luxury, genuine hospitality, and a timeless sense of dolce far niente, the mindful sweetness of slowing down and savoring the moment. All that’s left to do is follow your senses and let the landscape lead the way—or simply pop the cork on one of the Polvaro Estate’s wines to emulate the magic from home.

To learn more about Polvaro Estate and its captivating wines, visit https://www.tenutapolvaro.com/en/or follow @tenutapolvaro on Instagram.

title: The Limoncello Spritz Is Euro Summer in a Glass
summary:
Limoncello is having a long-overdue renaissance, and the liqueur is starring in spritzes all across Italy and beyond.

The post The Limoncello Spritz Is Euro Summer in a Glass appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As far as Italian institutions go, limoncello is relatively new. While its precise origins are unknown and somewhat contested—the Gulf of Naples, Amalfi Coast, and Sicily all claim bragging rights—the sweet, highly alcoholic lemon liqueur was likely invented in the early 20th century, growing in popularity until it became one of the most famous ways to end a long, leisurely Italian meal. (Grappa, another iconic Italian liqueur, dates back to the 14th century.) 

Even as the citrus digestif became known nationally and around the world, limoncello remained largely artisanal, with families throughout Southern Italy taking pride in their recipes and lemons. But industrialized, cloyingly sweet limoncellos made with less-than-fresh lemons have proliferated too, souring the drink’s reputation.

Now, a new wave of producers and drink makers are giving limoncello the respect it deserves—in cocktail form. Traditionally sipped or taken as a shot after dinner, limoncello is less known as an ingredient in mixed libations. But that’s changing, largely because of one drink in particular: the spritz.

The light, sunny limoncello spritz is currently one of the hottest cocktails in Italy, particularly in regions known for their lemons, like Amalfi and Capri. This summer at Pazziella, a Luxury Collection Hotel in Capri, the cocktail has become so popular that bartender Marco Gunetti created a “Limoncello Spritz Ritual,” offering guests a guided tasting of three different variations, with Gunetti providing tips for preparing them at home.

What makes these spritzes so special are the local lemons that produce the limoncello—a draw for tourists increasingly geared towards terroir and regional authenticity. “Capri lemons are a true expression of their unique territory,” says Gunetti. “The island’s mild climate, sea breeze, and mineral-rich soil give the fruit an exceptionally intense aroma and a peel naturally rich in essential oils.”

The Limoncello Renaissance

Beyond Capri and across Italy, the liqueur is trending, in part thanks to their spritz potential.

“Limoncello is definitely having a renaissance right now,” says Alessandro Buonadonna, head barman and mixologist director at Grand Hotel Villa Serbelloni on Lake Como. It’s increasingly playing a starring role in spritzes, which themselves are on the upswing. The limoncello spritz is made with the lemon liqueur, Prosecco, club soda, and mint leaves.

Buonadonna attributes the limoncello spritz’s popularity to its simplicity and the fruity synchronicity “of both Prosecco and limoncello, which leaves a delightful taste without dryness.” Heavy on its own, limoncello really shines with some dilution. “The citrusy kick of limoncello adds a vibrant and refreshing twist to the spritz,” he says. 

To make the drink at J.K. Place Capri, located in one of the great limoncello capitals of Italy, assistant restaurant manager Vincenzo Nappi insists upon using all-natural Limoncello di Capri, which is produced only with regionally certified Sorrento lemon peels, alcohol, water, and sugar. 

Although limoncello hails from many regions in Italy, he swears by bottles from the Sorrento coast made with artisanal methods that “respect the traditions and flavors of the island of Capri.” Sometimes Nappi will even modify the drink with strawberries to make a limoncello spritz rosso, which delivers a lovely pink hue.

On the nearby Amalfi coast, Hotel Poseidon Positano is also well-known for its limoncello spritz, which is made with limoncello produced via a treasured family recipe. “It works so well in a cocktail, particularly on warmer days, as it’s reminiscent of a lemon sorbet,” says Liliana Mascolo, one of the family members who owns and runs the hotel. “It’s refreshing and a little tart, with just the right amount of sweetness.”

Because it’s so unfussy, the limoncello spritz is an ideal summer cocktail to make at home. That said, each ingredient requires proper attention because there are so few. For the Prosecco, Buonadonna recommends a bubbly like Jeio by Bisol, an extra-dry bottle with “a fragrant and fruity nature that complements the citrus flavors of limoncello.” 

Choosing the Right Limoncello

As for the limoncello, there is no shortage of excellent options. “When choosing a limoncello, it is important to focus on the producers, and there are a few very interesting ones who have come along recently,” says Nicola Spaggiari, bar manager at Borgo Santo Pietro in Tuscany. These days, Spaggiara likes limoncello from Villa Massa, a Sorrento-based producer that uses hand-picked lemons, and Assuntina, a maker out of Capri that uses underripe lemons to make a bright-green limoncello.

Buonadonna is currently excited about Distilleria Cioffi, a producer based in Ravello, on the Amalfi Coast, which employs traditional methods like harvesting the lemons at dawn, at the peak of their flavor. The resulting flavor profile is “balanced, soft, and sweet, with a long, juicy citrus consistency,” Buonadonna says.

The renaissance has even migrated out of the south and across Italy, to places where limoncello traditionally has not been made. Scuppoz, one of Spaggiari’s favorite producers, is based in Abruzzo. Their limoncello is made with lemons grown on the Adriatic Coast, which offer a less-sweet profile than what you’ll find in Amalfi (and a higher alcohol content). 

The thirst for limoncello spritzes will only continue to grow, says Spaggiari, who is based in Tuscany, because it’s the perfect way to enjoy a traditional Italian product in the refreshing spritz format. But you don’t have to travel to Italy to drink it—just make the following recipe at home.

How to Make a Limoncello Spritz

Recipe courtesy of Hotel Poseidon Positano

  • 1 ⅔ ounces (50 ml) limoncello (such as Limoncello di Capri)
  • 2 ½ ounces (75 ml) Prosecco
  • ¾ ounces (25 ml) soda water
Step 1
Fill a long glass, ideally a wine or hurricane glass, with ice.
Step 2
Pour all the ingredients into the glass in the following order: limoncello, Prosecco, soda water.
Step 3
Stir well with a long spoon.
Step 4
Decorate with a lime or lemon slice and cherries.

title: Emidio Pepe’s Winemaking Ideas Were Old-Fashioned, Until They Were Radical
summary:
One day after his 94th birthday, the world lost an Italian wine legend who refused to modernize what didn't need improving.

The post Emidio Pepe’s Winemaking Ideas Were Old-Fashioned, Until They Were Radical appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When Emidio Pepe began bottling wine in Abruzzo in 1964, the Italian wine industry was heading rapidly in another direction. Stainless steel, mechanization, and modern enology promised cleaner, more consistent wines and a path toward the international market. He chose to remain true to himself, and his region.

Pepe, who died on July 28, one day after turning 94, would later be described as a pioneer of biodynamic and even natural wine. But perhaps his greater significance was that he remained a living bridge between two Italys: the agricultural world he was born into and the modern wine country that developed around him.

A Relic of a Kinder Past

Throughout his illustrious career, Pepe kept farming and making wine much as it had been done before industrialization. At his eponymous winery, vineyards were worked by hand and without synthetic chemicals. Whites were crushed by foot, reds destemmed by hand, and fermentations occurred spontaneously in glass-lined concrete, without filtration or added sulfites.

When I visited Pepe in Abruzzo in 2019, the language barrier meant we spoke little. Since he was already retired, his granddaughter Chiara de Iulis Pepe hosted me. But in some ways, watching him told me more. In his coppola (flat cap) and groomed mustache, moving through the rhythms of the day and, after lunch, sitting down with the newspaper, he seemed rooted in another era, shaped by vineyard work, meals, family, and familiar rituals. It was genuinely how he lived.

Perhaps that is what made Pepe so unusual. He never saw a reason to abandon the parts of tradition that worked.

That same stubborn continuity defined his wines. Pepe found a kindred spirit in Luigi Veronelli, the influential Italian writer who championed small farmers and believed wine should be cultivated, not manufactured. After Veronelli’s death, Chiara recalled one of the beliefs he and Pepe shared: “The smaller the estate, the tinier the vineyard, the more perfect the wine.”

That faith mattered in Abruzzo, where Montepulciano was largely sold in bulk or drunk locally. Starting with just 1.5 hectares, Pepe believed Montepulciano and Trebbiano could make profound, long-lived wines, a conviction that initially raised eyebrows even within his family.

Time vindicated him beautifully. From Veronelli’s legendary cellar, I tasted Pepe’s 1975 Montepulciano, still remarkably alive. Later, I bought his 1971 Trebbiano from the same collection. More than half a century after harvest, it was one of the finest bottles of white wine I have ever tasted: living proof that Pepe was ahead of his time.

And what once appeared old-fashioned eventually became radical again.

Ahead of ‘Natural Wine’

I saw that reversal firsthand three years before my visit to Abruzzo. In 2016, as New York’s natural wine scene was exploding, I attended Big Glou in Williamsburg. Among a young crowd excited about low-intervention winemaking were Pepe’s granddaughters, Chiara and Elisa, pouring wines made according to principles their grandfather had followed for more than half a century.

The irony was striking. Pepe hadn’t adapted to natural wine. It was the hipsters that just labeled his old-school approach as “natural.”

Time proved him right. Pepe routinely held back half of each vintage, sometimes much more. Over the years, his cellar became an archive of his convictions, vintage after vintage proving that Abruzzo’s native grapes possessed a longevity few had imagined.

“He lived an absolutely incredible life, full of all things,” Chiara told me after his death. “He felt he had to prove himself his whole life and towards the end he got the moral recognition he was looking for.”

By then, the wine world had changed around him, only to circle back toward ideas he had never abandoned. Chiara’s memories also revealed a man of simple pleasures: dancing the waltz, growing tomatoes, pruning fruit trees, eating spaghetti, driving his tractor, and, unexpectedly, enjoying New York street food. Perhaps they were all part of the same philosophy: to live closely, patiently, and with little concern for fashion.

His daughters, Sofia and Daniela, as well as his granddaughters, now carry that life’s work forward. “We feel the privilege to have had him in our lives and to have learnt from him,” Chiara said. “We will work relentlessly to honor the legacy he has left us.”

With Pepe’s death, Italian wine loses more than one of its great growers. It loses one of its last direct links to a world before wine became an industry, when the farmer, the vineyard, and the cellar were not separate ideas.

Emidio Pepe spent his life refusing to modernize what he believed didn’t need improving. In the end, modern wine came back around to him.

title: How Boisset Collection Celebrates the Bond Between French and American Winemaking
summary:
While companies devoted to championing Burgundian and Californian wines, respectively, are quick to debate what makes each region so nuanced and singular, few truly celebrate the deep link between French and American winemaking traditions and culture. For over five decades, family-owned Boisset Collection has successfully brought together more than 30 legendary wineries across California and

The post How Boisset Collection Celebrates the Bond Between French and American Winemaking appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
How Boisset Collection Celebrates the Bond Between French and American Winemaking

While companies devoted to championing Burgundian and Californian wines, respectively, are quick to debate what makes each region so nuanced and singular, few truly celebrate the deep link between French and American winemaking traditions and culture. For over five decades, family-owned Boisset Collection has successfully brought together more than 30 legendary wineries across California and Burgundy, as well as from Beaujolais, the Rhône Valley, and the South of France that share over 7,000 years of history.

As America celebrates its 250th anniversary, it’s an especially compelling time to reflect on the historic relationship that binds the two countries together.

By uniting iconic Burgundian names like Bouchard Aîné & Fils and Domaine de la Vougeraie to Californian icons like Buena Vista Winery, Raymond Vineyards, DeLoach Vineyards, and Elizabeth Spencer, Boisset cemented its position as one of the leading luxury names in Franco-American wine.

Additionally, Boisset Collection is a household name for prestige sparkling wines, including JCB Jean-Charles Boisset Crémant de Bourgogne and Champagne. 

Beyond a commitment to preserving each winery within its portfolio’s lasting legacy and heritage, the company’s focus on sustainability in farming and production has helped bring each estate proudly into the 21st century. 

Founder Jean-Charles Boisset personally initiated the implementation of biodynamic farming at all of the family’s estates. Boisset’s first estate vineyard in California, DeLoach Vineyards in Sonoma’s Russian River Valley is a renowned producer of Chardonnay, Zinfandel, and Pinot Noir, and it began its estate transition to regenerative agriculture in 2004.

Four years later, the winery received an organic seal of approval by California Certification of Organic Farmers (CCOF) and earned a biodynamic certification by Demeter just two years later. To mark its 50th anniversary vintage of Pinot Noir this year, DeLoach’s $50 bottles bear the label, “Made With Organic Grapes.”

Similarly, Raymond Vineyards was also certified CCOF and Demeter in 2013, making it the largest certified biodynamic estate on the Napa Valley floor. In accordance with the Demeter Biodynamic Farm Standard, Raymond set aside 10% of its estate to biodiversity, including the Theater of Nature, Napa Valley’s most comprehensive, interactive tour of biodynamic farming.

According to utility provider Blue Sky Utility, Raymond Vineyards is now the largest 100% solar-powered winery in Napa, boasting more than 50,000 square feet of panels on the winery’s roofs and a 17,000 square foot solar canopy.  

Boisset Collection’s commitment to sustainability crosses both sides of the pond. This stewardship and love of the land hails from the family’s deep roots in the French wine industry.

Born in the village of Vougeot, Jean-Charles’ passion for wine began as a child. He grew up above the cellars and within view of the centuries-old vineyards of Château du Clos de Vougeot, the epicenter and birthplace of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

His parents, Jean-Claude and Claudine, founded the family winery in 1961.

But it wasn’t until 1999 that Jean-Charles and his sister Nathalie teamed up to unite the family’s Burgundy vineyards, including prestigious monopoles such as the Vougeot 1er Cru Clos Blanc de Vougeot—planted in 1110 by the Cistercian monks—into what is now one of Burgundy’s leading domaines.

Domaine de la Vougeraie has been using biodynamic cultivation methods since its creation in 1999. As the leading organic and biodynamic domaine in the Côte d’Or, Domaine de la Vougeraie has more than 95 acres under cultivation.
